paragraphs.text: Gregory, Bishop of Nyssa: A Defence Addressed to His Brother Peter, on the Hexaemeron

Is this what you do, man of God? You urge [?] me to dare what should not be dared, and to take on tasks that cannot be achieved, and that cannot even be attempted without blame, in my judgment at least. In his account of the making of the world the great Moses taught, by divine inspiration, certain things that seem to contradict one another if the words are taken at their obvious meaning. You have told me to link these into a single consistent line of thought and to show that holy Scripture agrees with itself. And you ask this after our father's God-inspired treatment of the same subject, which everyone who knows it admires no less than the teaching of Moses himself. They are right to do so, I think. Think of how an ear of grain relates to its seed. It comes from the seed and yet is not the seed. Or rather, it is the seed in potential, but it differs in size, beauty, variety and shape. One might say that the thoughts which the great Basil drew out through his more painstaking study relate in the same way to the words of the great Moses.

Moses said these things in few words that are easily grasped. Our teacher enlarged them through his lofty philosophy and made of them not an ear of grain but a tree. It is like the mustard seed to which the Kingdom is compared, which grows into a tree in the heart of whoever tends it. His tree spreads out on every side with thoughts. Instead of branches it opens out into doctrines, and it reaches upward toward the goal of true religion. Its branches are so large that even lofty souls who soar on high, whom the Gospel calls the birds of the sky, can nest in them. For when the soul assents to the answer it was looking for, this is a kind of nest for it. The restless busyness of the mind finds rest there, like a bird ending a long and wandering flight. How then could anyone plant the small cutting [?] of my understanding beside so great a tree of words? Surely you are not asking for that, and I would never accept it: that my labour should be set up as a rival to the diligent work of our father and teacher. But farmers perform a kind of marvel when they ingeniously produce different fruits on a single plant. This is how they do it. They strip a small bud from one tree, together with the bark at its base. Then they cut into the bark of another, larger plant at a single spot and fit the bud into it. The natural sap of the larger plant nourishes what has been inserted, and it grows into a branch. In the same way I will graft my understanding, like a small shoot, into the sap of that great tree, the wisdom of our teacher. I will try to become a branch of it, growing into its thoughts as far as I can and watered by the starting points it supplies. For I think some people have not rightly understood the purpose of his work on the Hexaemeron. That is why they complain that he gave them no clear account of the sun: how this luminary was made, along with the other stars, only after three days had passed. They argue that a day cannot be marked off by morning and evening unless the sun produces evening by setting and morning by rising. Likewise they do not accept the creation of two heavens. They say that even though the Apostle mentions a third heaven, the difficulty on this point remains. One heaven was made in the beginning, and after that the firmament. But Moses does not record another heaven, that is, a second act of creation. So there is no proof that we should think of a third heaven beyond these two. No other heaven came into being after the firmament, and the word "beginning" does not allow us to suppose that anything came before. For if heaven came into being in the beginning, then clearly creation began at that point. Scripture would not have called it a beginning if it had some other beginning above it, because what comes second in order neither is a beginning nor is called one. And yet Paul mentions a third

heaven, which the creation account does not contain. So here too, the mention of a second heaven is one of the points in question. Those who raise these and similar objections do not seem to me to have considered the purpose of our father's teaching. He was addressing a great crowd of people in a packed church, so he had to suit his words to his listeners. Among so many hearers, many could follow loftier discussions. But many times more could not keep up with a subtler examination of ideas. There were unlearned men and artisans busy with sedentary trades. There were the women of the congregation, who had no training in such studies, and there were the young children and the elderly. All of these needed teaching that would lead them by the hand, with a delight they could easily grasp, through the visible creation and its beauties to the knowledge of the One who made all things. So if you judge what he said by the purpose of the great teacher, nothing is missing from it. He did not compose a combative treatise that eagerly wrestled with objections. He gave himself wholly to a simpler explanation of the words, so that his teaching would suit the simplicity of his hearers. Yet at the same time his explanation somehow rose to the level of his more capable listeners, as he displayed the varied learning of secular philosophy. So the many understood him, and the most gifted admired him. But you are like someone who leaves the great crowd of people below on Mount Sinai. Raised in mind above the rest, you are eager to enter, together with the great Moses, into the darkness where unspeakable things are contemplated. There he saw what cannot be seen and heard words that cannot be spoken. And you want to know the necessary order of creation. When heaven and earth had come into being, how is it that light waited for the divine command before it came to be, while darkness existed even without a command? And if light needed nothing else to brighten the air beneath it and to divide time into night and day, what need was there to make the sun? And if the earth came into being with heaven from the beginning, how could what had come into being be unformed? For "forming" and "making" seem to mean the same thing. If then making is the same as forming, how can what has been made be unformed? Then there are the difficulties about the watery substance. They say it is impossible for a liquid to rest above the vault of heaven, since the vault is shaped like a sphere. How could moisture settle on a convex surface? By every necessity the liquid would flow away from the highest point of the sphere toward its sloping sides. And since its base gives it no stability, how could it stay in place itself, when it is always slipping off its own base? And how could it avoid being scattered, when the extremely swift revolution of the heavenly pole must throw off whatever sits on it? Moreover, the objectors find it implausible that the watery element is used up, because

bodies of water are always seen at the same level, in springs, rivers and lakes alike. The exception is certain springs whose supply of water lies near the surface and comes from the seepage of rain or snow. Like torrents, these dry up and swell along with the inflow from above. But where a stream pours out without ceasing and neither shrinks nor grows, we must admit that nothing of the watery substance is being used up. For what is being consumed cannot stay at the same level forever. Nor, if fire really consumed water, would it have stayed at its own measure without growing and without nourishment. For fire cannot fail to grow along with the matter it consumes. So you busy yourself with these and similar questions, reaching out toward everything lofty, and you want to see with your own mind what lies in the darkness of Moses' vision. If so, you should look not to someone else but to the grace that is in you. You should search out the depths of God through the spirit of revelation, which is made manifest to you through prayer. But the apostolic law requires us to yield to one another in love, and a servant earns praise by carrying out what he is told. So I will try, as briefly as I can, to set out my view on these matters, and I will have your prayer as my ally in the discussion. But before I begin, let me solemnly declare this. I lay down no doctrine that contradicts holy Basil's teaching on the making of the world, even if my reasoning should lead by some chain of argument to a different interpretation. His views must prevail and rank second only to the divinely inspired Testament. Readers should take what I offer as exercises attempted in the manner of the schools, as in a gymnasium. If anything in what I say is found to depart from common opinion, let no one be harmed by it. I do not offer my discussion as dogma, which would give slanderers a handle against me. I admit that I am only exercising my own mind on the ideas set before me, not laying down an authoritative interpretation for those who come after. So let no one demand that I grapple with the objections raised against us from holy Scripture, or with the points in our teacher's ready explanations [?] that seem not to agree with common notions. That is not my purpose: to devise some defence against contradictions that appear at first glance. Rather, let me be free to examine the sense of the words with my own aim in view. Perhaps, with God's help, I may be able to work out a connected and consistent account of how created things came to be, while leaving the wording its proper meaning. "In the beginning," it says, "God made the heaven and the earth," and so on through everything the account of the making of the world contains. These are the things that came into being in the six days. But before examining what is written, I think the argument must first establish

this point. In the divine nature, power goes together with will, and God's will is the measure of His power. And His will is wisdom. It belongs to wisdom to know fully how each thing may come to be. And power is joined by nature to this knowledge. So as soon as He knew what ought to come to be, the strength that brings beings into existence was there at once. It brought what had been conceived into actuality and did not lag behind the knowledge in any way. The work is displayed together with the plan, joined to it without any interval. For the plan is at the same time a power. It works out beforehand how beings are to come to be, and it supplies the means for what has been conceived to exist. So in creation all that belongs to God is to be thought of together: the will, the wisdom, the power, and the substance of the things that exist. Since this is so, no one need any longer be at a loss when investigating matter, asking how it came to be and where it came from. One hears people say such things as: "If God is immaterial, where does matter come from? How can what has quantity come from what has none, the visible from the invisible, and what is bounded throughout by bulk and size from what has no magnitude and no limits? And all the other properties seen in matter: how, or from where, did He produce them, when He has nothing of the kind in His own nature?" There is one answer to every objection raised against us about matter. We must neither suppose that God's wisdom lacks power nor that His power lacks wisdom. These two go together and are shown to be one, so that each is seen along with the other, at once and in the same respect. His wise will was made manifest by the power of what was accomplished, and His active power was brought to completion in His wise will. If then wisdom and power are one and the same, He neither lacks the knowledge of how matter might be found for the making of beings, nor lacks the ability to bring what He has conceived into actuality. Since He can do all things, by His wise and powerful will He laid down all at once everything through which matter exists, for the production of beings: lightness, heaviness, density, rarity, softness, resistance, wetness, dryness, cold, heat, color, shape, outline, extension. Taken by themselves, all of these are concepts and bare ideas. None of them by itself is matter, but when they come together they become matter. If then, by the supremacy of His wisdom and power, He both knows all things and can do all things, perhaps we come closer to the lofty words of Moses, who says that heaven and earth were made by God "in summary." (This is how Aquila rendered the word translated "beginning.") For the prophet wrote the book of Genesis as an introduction to the knowledge of God. Moses' aim is to lead those who are enslaved to the senses by the hand, through visible things, to what lies beyond the grasp of sense perception. Now what we know through sight is bounded by heaven and earth. For this reason the text names the outer limits of what we know through the senses, as things that contain all that exists. By saying that God made what contains, it includes everything contained within those limits.

Instead of saying that God made all beings at once, it says that God made the heaven and the earth "in summary," or "in the beginning." The two words, "beginning" and "summary," have one meaning. Both equally indicate that all came about at once. "Summary" presents all things as coming into being together, while "beginning" indicates something instantaneous, with no interval. For a beginning has nothing to do with the idea of extension. As the point is the beginning of a line, and the atom the beginning of bulk, so the instant is the beginning of an interval of time. So when the ineffable power of God laid down all beings at once, Moses called it the "beginning" or "summary" in which the whole is said to have been constituted. He named the outer limits of beings and silently indicated what lies between along with them. I call them limits because of human sense perception, which neither penetrates beneath the earth nor passes beyond heaven. So the beginning of the account of the making of the world teaches us this. In an instant God laid down together the starting points, the causes and the powers of all beings. In the first impulse of His will the substance of every being came together: heaven, ether, stars, fire, air, sea, earth, animal, plants. All these were seen by the divine eye, shown forth by the word of His power, since, as the prophecy says, He "knows all things before they come to be." Power and wisdom had been laid down together so that each part of the world might be brought to completion. A necessary sequence followed from this, in a certain order. Fire came first and appeared before the other things seen in the universe. Next came what necessarily follows what came before. After that came a third thing, as the skilful order of nature required, then a fourth and a fifth, and the rest in their sequence. They did not appear by some accidental chance, by a disorderly and random motion. Moses says that each thing came to be as the necessary order of nature demands a proper sequence among things coming into being. In this way he set forth the teachings of natural philosophy in the form of a narrative. He also adds certain commands spoken by God for each thing that came to be, and in this too he did well and spoke as befits God. For everything that comes to be through God's ordered sequence and wisdom is plainly a kind of utterance. We do not know what God's essence is. But when we grasp in thought [?] wisdom itself and power itself, we believe that we have grasped God in our understanding. This is why darkness was poured over the universe when the whole had come into being, before each of the things that make up the whole had been shown forth separately. For the brightness of fire had not yet come out, but lay hidden in the particles of matter. Flints likewise remain unseen in the dark, even though by nature they hold the power to give light and produce fire when struck against each other. When a spark leaps out of them, they too appear in its glow. In the same way, all things were invisible and unseen before the substance that gives light came out into view. For the universe had only just come into existence all at once, in the single movement of the divine will,

and was still undistinguished, with all the elements mixed up with one another. So the fire scattered everywhere was darkened, blocked by the great mass of matter. But its power is keen and quick to move. As soon as God gave the nature of beings the signal for the world to come into being, it leapt out ahead of everything heavier, and at once everything was lit up with light. What came about through the power of the Maker, in accordance with the principle of wisdom, Moses recorded as a word of command from God: "God said, Let there be light, and there was light." For with God, at least as I understand it, the deed is the word. Everything that comes to be comes to be by a rational word. Nothing irrational, accidental or spontaneous can be thought of among the things that owe their existence to God. Rather, we must believe that a wise and skilful principle lies within each being, even if it is beyond our sight. Since the expression "God said" points to a word, we shall understand it, I think, in a way worthy of God if we refer the text to the principle inherent in creation. This is how the great David explained such expressions to us when he said, "You made all things in wisdom." Moses wrote down, as coming from the divine voice, the words that commanded beings to be created. David called these the wisdom that is seen in the things that have been made. That is why he also says that the heavens declare the glory of God. He means that the skilful design shown in them through their harmonious revolution serves as speech for those who have understanding. Having said that the heavens declare and the firmament proclaims, he corrects those who take his words too crudely and perhaps expect the heavens' declaration to produce the sound of a voice and articulate speech. So he says: "There is no speech nor words; their voices are not heard." This shows that the wisdom seen in creation is speech, even though it is not articulate. Again, Moses says that God addressed detailed utterances to him while the wonders of the signs in Egypt were being worked. The Psalmist explained this at a higher level than common opinion when he said, "He set among them the words of His signs, and of His wonders in the land of Ham." By this phrase the Psalmist plainly hinted that the power which produces each thing that happens is brought into action by a kind of word. The word does not consist of spoken utterances; rather, the power at work in the signs is given this name. So here too the power that gives light ran ahead and separated itself from the other beings by the swiftness and mobility of its nature. It set itself apart from things of a different nature, and everything it shone upon was lit up by its radiant power. But by what principle the substance of fire does these things, God alone can say, who placed the principle of light-giving within its nature. And this, through his own writing, also [?]

[?] Moses bears witness to this where he says, "And God said, Let there be light." By these words, I think, he gives us to understand that the work of light is a divine word, one that passes beyond all human understanding. We look only at what comes to be, and we take in the wonder through our senses. But where fire dwells before it is suddenly brought forth, we cannot see. If it leaps out when pebbles strike together, we cannot see from what pebbles it comes, or from what other substance when that is rubbed against itself. Nor can we see, or form any notion of, the power that devours whatever it has seized and lights up the air with its flame. Instead we say that the reason for this astonishing wonder is stored up in God alone. It was he who made it so, by the ineffable reason of his power, that light should be born with fire. So Moses testifies in his own account: "And God said, Let there be light, and there was light; and God saw the light, that it was good." For truly it belongs to God alone to see how a thing so good could come to be. The poverty of our nature sees what comes to be, but it can neither see nor praise the reason by which it comes to be. Praise belongs to things that are known, not to things unknown. "God saw," then, he says, "the light, that it was good, and God divided between the light and the darkness." Here again Moses refers to divine activity something that happens necessarily, in a certain order and harmony, as nature follows its course. By these words, I think, he teaches that God's wisdom had foreseen everything that was to come about in sequence through a necessary order. The luminous substance that had been scattered through the universe ran together to what was akin to it and was all gathered about itself. When that happened, whatever the rest of the elements' matter screened off was necessarily cast into shadow, and that shadow was darkness. This came about in natural sequence. So that no one would attribute it to some spontaneous chance, Moses says it is the work of God, who placed this power in the things that came to be. And indeed, it is plain to everyone from what we see that the nature of fire is swift, rising and ever-moving. But what the account suggests we should understand as following from this beginning, Moses wrote down as history, in the form of a narrative: "And there was evening, and there was morning." For who does not know this? Creation is understood to be twofold, the intelligible and the sensible. The lawgiver's whole concern here is not to explain intelligible things but to show us the ordering of sensible things through what we can see. Now, as soon as the universe was constituted, fire was shot out like an arrow from the elements of a different nature. By the upward and light character of its natural motion it sprang out ahead of the whole and passed through the sensible substance as swiftly as thought. But it could not carry its motion onward in a straight line, because the intelligible creation does not mix with sensible things, and fire is sensible. For this reason

fire, having reached the outermost bounds of creation, necessarily moves in a circle. The power inherent in its nature drives it ever onward, but there is no room for motion in a straight line, since all sensible creation is enclosed within its own bounds. So it travels along the outermost limit of sensible nature, where it can move freely, because the intelligible nature, as we said before, does not admit fire's course into itself. For this reason Moses followed the motion of fire in thought and says that the light which came into being did not stay in the same parts. Instead, it encircles the denser substance of things, and by the force of its revolving motion it brings brightness in turn to the parts without light and gloom to those that had been lit. And perhaps it is because this succession, of light and of darkness I mean, happens in the lower region at intervals of time, that Moses again ascribes to God the naming of day and night. He does not let us think that anything which came about in sequence did so of itself, or had its beginning from anything else. That is why he says, "God called the light day, and the darkness he called night." The illuminating power is by nature unable to stay still. So when the brightness had passed through the upper part of the circle and was moving toward what lay below, what lay above was necessarily cast into shadow as the fire ran beneath, presumably because the denser nature blocked the radiance. This withdrawal of light he named evening. And when the fire had run round the lower circle and brought its radiance back to the upper parts, he called what happened morning, giving that name to the dawn. Let us briefly go back over the argument, so that the passages of divine Scripture we have cited may support the coherence of the interpretation we have given. The account of the world's creation said at the very beginning, "In the beginning God made the heaven and the earth." We took this to mean that the account presents the constitution of all things at once, pointing by what contains to what is within as well. For the middle is wholly enclosed by the extremes, and the extremes, as far as human perception goes, are heaven and earth, since human sight is bounded by these on either side. The one who said, "In his hand are the ends of the earth," included the middle as well in the compass of the ends. In the same way Moses indicated the material foundation of the whole world by its limits. And we say that the words in between support this interpretation. For it is written, "And the earth was invisible and unformed." From this it is clear that all things existed in potency in God's first impulse toward creation, as though a kind of seminal power had been laid down for the coming-to-be of the universe, while the individual things did not yet exist in actuality. For the earth, he says, was invisible and unformed. This

is the same as saying that it was, and was not, for the qualities had not yet come together around it. The proof of this meaning is that the account calls it invisible. What is invisible has no color. Color arises as a kind of emanation from the shape of a surface, and there is no shape without body. If, then, it was invisible, it was certainly colorless as well. Shapelessness goes with colorlessness, and bodilessness with shapelessness. So when the world was founded all at once, the earth was indeed among the things that existed, as were all the others. But it was still waiting for what comes through being furnished with qualities, that is, for coming into being. By calling it invisible, the account shows that no other quality could be observed in it either. And by calling it unformed, it gives us to understand that it had not yet been made dense with bodily properties. This meaning is made still clearer by the versions of Symmachus, Theodotion and Aquila. One of them says, "The earth was idle and undistinguished"; another, "Emptiness and nothing"; and the third, "Nothing and nothing." In my view, "idle" shows that it did not yet exist in actuality but had its being in potency alone. "Undistinguished" shows that the qualities had not yet separated from one another, and that none of them could yet be recognized individually by itself. The whole was seen in a confused and undistinguished quality: no color, no shape, no bulk, no weight, no size, nor anything else of the kind could be observed in the substrate by itself according to its own principle. "Emptiness and nothing" shows us the same meaning. By the word "emptiness" he indicated the capacity to receive qualities. We learn from this that the creator of the universe laid down beforehand a potency able to receive qualities, but that it was empty and had nothing in itself before it was filled with qualities. The third rendering I think I should leave unexamined, since it seems to have been borrowed from the philosophy of Epicurus. For he too says something similar about the first principle of things. With words like these he points to the insubstantial nature of the atoms as empty sound and nothing, which is much like "nothing and nothing." But let us go on again with the rest of our inquiry. Once fire had gone round the outermost bound of sensible nature, how did the firmament come into being as a consequence, which Scripture says is the boundary between the waters above and the waters below? I do not think that any solid and resistant body is to be seen in the firmament, whether one of the four elements or some other besides these, as pagan philosophy imagined. Rather, the outermost limit of sensible substance, round which the nature of fire patrols with its ever-moving power, is what Scripture calls the firmament. It calls it that by comparison with the eternal, bodiless and intangible nature. For who does not know that everything solid has been made dense by some kind of resistance? What is dense and resistant is not free of the quality of weight, and what is heavy by nature cannot rise upward. But the firmament lies above all sensible creation. Therefore

the logic of the argument does not allow us to think of anything thick or bodily in it. As has been said, everything of the sensible kind is called solid by contrast with what is intelligible and bodiless, even if its natural fineness escapes our perception. It follows, then, that whatever was encompassed by the fire's revolution was given a name. What it encompassed was the limit of material substance, once that had been circumscribed by a bound of its own. It was called firmament because of its material nature, by comparison with the things discussed above [?]. And it received the name heaven, just as he gave light the name day and darkness the name night. The division of the waters, which the firmament separates by standing between them, is not foreign to this interpretation and agrees with Scripture. For in the order of the narrative, after speaking of the earth, it is written: "Darkness was over the abyss, and the Spirit of God was borne above the water." We infer, then, that the Spirit of God is as far from being darkness as it is estranged from all evil. Countless sayings of holy Scripture could be cited on this point: that God is true light, and that he dwells in unapproachable light. The Spirit of God is the same in nature as God himself. If God and the Spirit have one nature, and God is light, then the Spirit of God must surely be light as well. And light surely brings into light the things over which it is borne. So the water over which the Spirit of God was borne is something other than the downward-tending nature of flowing waters. The firmament walls it off from the heavy, downward-tending water. Scripture does call that too water, and we infer, by a higher contemplation, that it signifies the fullness of the intelligible powers. Let no one be thrown by the shared name. For God too is a consuming fire, yet the word is free of the material meaning of fire. When you learned that God is fire, you understood him to be something other than this fire. In the same way, when you are taught about water over which the divine Spirit is borne, do not think of the downward-tending nature that flows down to the earth. For the Spirit of God is not borne over what is low and unstable. So that the thought may be laid open more clearly to us, let us briefly sum up the sense of what has been said. The firmament, which was called heaven, is the boundary of sensible creation. Beyond it there follows an intelligible creation. In it there is no form, no magnitude, no position in place, no measure by dimensions, no color, no shape, no size, nor anything at all of the things seen under heaven. And let no one suspect me of confusing the study of the text with figurative interpretation, as if I agreed with the conjectures of those before us who have interpreted such things. They say that the apostate powers are called the abyss, and that the world-ruler of darkness is meant by the darkness over the abyss. May I never so transgress as to think evil a creation of God! The divine word says clearly in its summing-up, "And God saw all the things that he had made, and

so as to think, and be convinced, that the nature of each is different. The one is upward-tending and light, lighter even than fire is. It therefore stays above the hot substance. It is not carried along with the motion of what lies beneath it, nor is it driven by the heat into the opposite position. It remains undiminished itself and gives the fire running beneath it no passage through itself. For how could the immaterial become a place for the material? The other water is the one whose nature we know by sight, touch and taste. It moves downward, it is seen to be transparent, and it is known to the taste by the quality within it. The nature of something so well known does not compel us to transfer it to some other meaning. But consider the other thing called water. It is neither seen nor flowing, nor is it held at all by the things that naturally contain liquids. It is outside place and unmixed with every quality known through the senses. It is borne beneath the Spirit of God, it is believed to be above the heavens, and it remains outside everything known through the senses. For these reasons I do not think anyone practiced in judgment would take it to be anything but something other than ordinary water, and would refer it in thought to the intelligible substance. From what we have examined we inferred that everything in motion is enclosed within bounds short of the intelligible nature and turns back upon itself. The boundary for things in motion is the limit of the nature that has dimensions. Beyond it is found the intelligible nature, which has no dimensions and is free of all spatial and dimensional properties. So the outermost limit of sensible substance, beyond which there is nothing of the kind known in things that appear, is what we say is meant by the name firmament. Scripture confirms our inference where it says, "And God divided between the water that was below the firmament and the water that was above the firmament." These words show that the one water had never been mixed with the other, even from the beginning. Though

they shared a name, their nature was unmixed. For Scripture does not say "came to be below" or "was above the firmament"; it says that what was below the firmament was one thing, and what was above was another. The one was marked off from the first in gloom, in the lower position. The other is not in gloom, for what is in the Spirit of God is certainly in light and is separated from gloom. And at the same time it was above the firmament that was shown to lie between them. Let the intelligent listener judge whether our account has arrived at a fitting interpretation in what has been said. These, then, are the conjectures we have made about the first constitution of things, and others like them. We have shown how light is not secondary among beings in the power of its being [?], even if Scripture says that darkness is recorded before light. We have set out our conjectures about the firmament, and about the difference between the waters. Their nature is divided into the downward-tending and the light, and this gives us fitting conjectures about each of the two things that bear the same name. So the waters were separated from one another, the seen and the conceived. Heaven was shown to be the middle boundary between the twofold nature of the waters. It is said to have come into being in the beginning together with the earth and all the things laid down for furnishing the world, but it was now completed and named when the firmament, defined by the circuit of fire, was made manifest. Then the second circuit of light again darkened and lit up the lower region in turn. And this too was named day, following the earlier pattern. The nature of number also necessarily entered creation as a consequence. For number is nothing other than a putting-together of units, and everything seen within a definite outline is called a unit. Since the circle is complete on every side and bounded in itself, the account rightly called one revolution of the circle one, saying, "There was evening and there was morning, one day." The next revolution it likewise called one. Putting both together, it made two. In this way the account joined the coming-to-be of number to the parts of creation, marking the order of the sequence by the names of the numbers. "There was," he says, "evening, and there was morning, a second day." Once these things had come about, the nature of things again went on in sequence and brought about what necessarily follows from what had come before. This work too is preceded by a divine command. Everywhere Moses makes our understanding secure, so that we think nothing that exists has been constituted without God, and so that the wonder of each thing made may be referred to its maker. All the luminous and fiery substance had been separated from the rest by its own qualities. Yet the furnishing of the air is passed over in silence. It would have been reasonable to explain the air's nature second, after the ascent of the [?]. For it has a certain kinship with fire in lightness, since lightness is seen in fire as well. And it would then have been reasonable to describe the heavy [?] nature. But Moses tells of

this, while he passes over the air in his account [?] mixture [?], and it gathers itself together, pressed into the hollows of the earth. Since, then, a thing of this kind belongs to divine power and wisdom, Moses says that a word of God led the way in this wonder, and he sets out a commanding utterance. But as I judge the matter, by this expressive [?] utterance he points to the principle inherent in the nature of creation. "God said," he tells us, "Let the waters be gathered into their gatherings,

and let the dry land appear." You see the necessary order of nature. When the water is drawn off the earth, what is separated from the moisture dries out. And since the moisture is no longer mixed with the earth into mud, the water is necessarily enclosed in certain receptacles. Otherwise, because of its fluid nature, it would come to vanish, with nothing to confine its spreading. But it seems to me not out of place to mention again the waters above the heavens. Here the earth is necessarily shaped to receive the waters. It encloses their fluidity in bays, as it were, and by its own steadiness it gives stability to the unstable nature of water. If so, how could that water, if it really is water, stand on what is unstable and stay unspilled on what is convex? For if we suppose that the two waters have one and the same nature, we are bound to think that what we see in the one holds for the other as well. So then the back of heaven must be split into channels, cut into ravines like the gaps between cliffs on earth, so that the water may be held in the hollows! And what will they say when the circular revolution of the celestial sphere tilts downward what is now uppermost? Will they not have to invent lids for the circles, so that the water does not hang down and flow out of the hollows? But he says that fire is consuming. It needs some matter that keeps feeding the flame, so that it does not die down and consume itself for lack of fuel. As for me, even if the great voice of our teacher agrees with this opinion, I shall ask my readers not to take it amiss if, looking to the logic of the argument, I do not follow in every respect those who have gone before me in the study of nature. For our teacher's aim was not at all to lay down his own opinions as law for his hearers. He wanted his disciples to gain through his teaching some approach to the truth. And so we, trained in the lessons he left behind, look to the logic of the argument. If this argument arrives at what is probable, the credit would go to the teacher's wisdom. What, then, do we reason in reply to the objection that has been raised? We see opposing qualities not only in fire and water. In each of the elements one can find some conflict between their properties and their opposites. In the elements just mentioned, heat opposes cold and dryness opposes moisture. In the same way, along the other diameter, the qualities in earth and in air are opposed and set against one another: solidity and looseness, resistance and rarity, heaviness and lightness. Whatever else is peculiar to each of these is known from its opposite. In these cases, then, it cannot be said that one is nourished by its opposite. The lightness in air does not grow by consuming what is heavy, nor does the compactness of earth produce [?] the rarity of its counterpart, nor do the remaining

…whose properties nourish the [?] qualities by being consumed themselves. In the same way one might say that the moist and the cold are indeed opposed to the hot and the dry, but that these are not nourished by each other's destruction, and that neither has its power to exist in the other's not existing. If that were so, neither would exist, since the survival of each would depend on the destruction of the other. The power to destroy the other is equal in each, and whichever prevails always does away with the one that falls short. That this account is true can be learned from experience itself. When fire has taken hold of some material and water is then poured on, you can plainly see these two destroying each other: whichever of them prevails wipes out the other, as each gives way to the superior force of what comes against it. As long as the strength of the two is evenly balanced, the destruction works equally from both sides, and neither is nourished by the other; the two simply vanish into each other. With beasts that devour one another, it is not in the nature of things for both to live off each other when each is destroying the other. In the same way the opposition of moist to dry would keep neither in existence if the loss of one were what nourished the other. But I think it better to take up our discussion in proper order, as follows. Since all the things that God made are very good, I say that the perfection of the good must be observed in each existing thing. The addition of "very", by its intensive force, clearly indicates a completeness that lacks nothing. Among living creatures one can see countless differences between their kinds, yet we say that the general verdict of approval on existing things applies to each of them, so that each is equally "very good". This approval does not concern appearance, for otherwise the centipede, the land frog, and the creatures that are born from rotting mud could hardly be called "very good". When the divine eye looks on created things, it does not judge goodness by their beauty, by fine color or comely shape, but by each thing, just as it is, having its nature complete in itself. The horse does not exist because the ox does not exist. Rather, nature preserves itself in each of them, having its own means of survival, and its power to exist lies not in the destruction of another nature. So even if the elements are differently disposed toward one another, each is still very good in itself. In itself, according to its own principle, each is filled with goodness. The earth is good, for it does not need the destruction of the air in order to be earth. It remains in its own qualities and preserves itself through the natural power that God placed in it. The air is good, not because the earth does not exist, but in being what it is, sufficient for its own survival by the powers naturally inherent in it. So too water is very good, and fire is very good, each filled with its own qualities, and each remaining forever by the power of the divine will, according to the proper measures of the first creation. "The earth," it says, "stands forever," neither diminished nor increased. The air is kept within its own bounds, and fire is not lessened. How then can water alone, of all things, be among the things that are consumed?

Besides this, we see that the fiery substance and power is great compared with other existing things. Those who have studied the heavenly bodies have clearly demonstrated that the sun is many times larger than the earth. As a result the earth's shadow does not reach far into the air, because the sun's overwhelming size, as its rays strike, narrows that shadow into a cone. Water, then, is so small when judged against the sun that, measured together with the whole earth, it is a tiny fraction of the sun's size. How long would this little amount have lasted, if so great a fire were consuming it? Yet we see the sea always full to the same level, and the flow of rivers keeping within its own measures. Experience of this kind therefore testifies that none of the moisture is consumed. At the beginning fire did not come into being through the destruction of moisture, but was brought into existence by the same power. In the same way, according to the original constitution of the element, its survival will be preserved forever, and the moist nature will not trouble the survival of fire. "But," they say, "we often see the earth soaked by a rainstorm, and then, when the sun has heated the ground more strongly, what was drenched a little before becomes dry. Where then," they say, "is the moisture in these things, if the heat of the sun's ray has not entirely consumed it?" By that reasoning, if the water in a jar were poured into another vessel and the full jar suddenly became empty, they would say that, since the water is not in this jar, it does not exist at all, even though it is now in another. Whoever supposes that what happens in that case also happens in this one will not miss the likely truth. It is the same thing for a liquid to flow from this vessel into another, and for the moisture of the earth to evaporate and be carried up into the air. When the heat above draws the moisture to itself, it naturally filters upward from the earth in fine particles. What happens can be seen from this evidence. Often, when thicker vapors are given off from the depths of the earth, something like a cloud seems to well up, and the vapors become so thick that they can be seen with the eyes. At other times the exhalation of moisture may be finer, so that it is in a way equal to the air in fineness. Then it is not visible to the eye until the exhalation of such moisture has gathered together and so become a cloud by being compressed. Thus the fine, vaporous droplets float on the air for a while because of their lightness and ride on the winds. But if more of the kindred moisture flows together into the mass and it becomes heavy, it falls out of the air onto the earth and becomes a drop. So the heat did not consume what it drew up from the earth. The cloud was formed from these vapors, and the cloud, when compressed, became water. This water, mingled with the earth again, was drawn up into vapor, and the vapor, formed into cloud, became rain. From this the earth again gave forth vapors, and these, thickened in the compression

of the clouds, flowed down. What flowed down was given off again as vapor, and so a kind of circle comes about, turning back on itself and always going around and revolving through the same stages. Whether you speak of plants or of shoots, everything goes round in this same circle. For the moisture runs up through the plants or seeds together with the shoots. It then leaves whatever earthy matter has come with it in the body of what it nourishes, and when that substance is dried by the surrounding air, the moisture evaporates again to join its own kind. The air is rarefied in its parts and finer even than the fine vapors, so it lets everything that comes into it pass through to what is akin to it. So dust, even if it is held up in the air for a long time, is given back to the earth. Moisture too is not lost: it finds [?] whatever is akin to it and of its own kind wandering in the air. It joins with this, grows by the addition of like particles, swells again until it forms a cloud, and so through drops is restored to its own nature. In this way the elements seen throughout the universe are everywhere kept at the same measure that the Creator's wisdom appointed for each existing thing at the beginning, for the harmony of the whole. But I know the opposing argument. In fiercer heat one can often see certain clouds scattered through the air, and anyone who watches them for a while will in a way refute this argument, which says that nothing of the moist nature is consumed. The clotted pieces of cloud scattered here and there in the air first shrink in bulk, baked by the excess of the blaze. Then they vanish completely, parched by the heat, so that not even a small remnant is left, because the blaze has dried up the moisture. This can no longer be explained by the account of vapors. The region above the clouds lies above this murky and windy air, and in the fineness of its own nature it admits nothing heavier. All vapors and all exhalations have as the limit of their upward movement the thickness of the air around the earth at that level, which by nature they cannot pass through. Nothing of the coarser matter could remain in what is fine and ethereal. For this reason those who have explored the summits of certain very high mountains say that these are always above the clouds and beyond the reach of the winds. Birds cannot fly up there, any more than underwater creatures can live in the air. From all this it is clearly shown that there is a kind of boundary in the air, facing the region above, which fixes the limit for all the coarser exhalations rising from the earth. That is why the snow on the summits stays unmelted even into summer: the vapors gathering at that level continually chill the air. Moreover, the experts in these matters explain that the fiery trails some call shooting stars arise from the same cause. When some of the thicker and more material air is forced up into the ethereal region by the violence of certain winds, it bursts into flame as soon as it gets up there, and the flame is carried flowing along by the impulse the wind has given it,

and when the wind dies down, the flame also fades away with it. "So the argument [?] can no longer claim that vapors form again when the cloud disappears, so that through them, as in the cases mentioned above, one might hope for the return of the moisture that was taken up. One must therefore agree with those who teach that the moisture is burnt up and passes into non-existence." For my part, I am persuaded that the moisture in the vapors does vanish through the excessive blaze, for I judge it vain and contentious to fight against what is evident. But since it is right not to tire of tracking down the truth from every side, I say that even though these things happen, the measure of the moist nature is kept undiminished, and whatever is consumed is always fully replaced for what is lacking. What makes me confident of this view is the following. From the action of fire among us we learn by experience that fire does not feed on all the qualities of a material, but only on the one it takes hold of. Take oil, for example. Because it [?] is free of the cold quality, the moisture in this material is easily drawn out by the heat of the fire and becomes flame. But the oil is not only changed into flame by the fire. The moisture of the fire that arises from the oil, it is said, becomes dry dust once the fire has done its work. The soot from a lamp clearly shows this, for it blackens whatever is above the flame. If this goes on longer, a kind of deposit even builds up [?] on the place the soot has blackened. From this it is clear that oil, dried out by the fire, is changed into fine and invisible particles, and in this form it passes into the air and from there settles onto the earth. That soot is finely spread through the air is shown by the nostrils of those who breathe this air turning black. Often too what is coughed up from the chest is seen to be black, because it is stained by the color of the soot that enters along with the air we breathe. It is clear from this, then, that the moisture of the oil was turned into dryness, while the bulk of its matter did not vanish into non-existence but was scattered through the air in fine and invisible particles. From what happens to this liquid we have learned that the moist is only changed into dryness, and its material does not vanish entirely. Anyone who applies this to the whole will not miss the likely truth, for it is clear that the whole is made up of parts. Whatever we have learned about the part, we have also been taught about the whole. And not even a contentious person would deny that moisture is one in kind. Now this moisture, burnt by fire, became fine dust. Therefore all moisture that comes into fire also changes the quality of its particles, passing from moist to dry, and does not vanish entirely. A cloud, then, is a mass of vapor, and vapor is the fine exhalation of moisture. So when the cloud is parched by the blaze, that fine and indivisible bulk of vapor may not keep its moist quality, but its underlying substance must not pass into extinction or dissolve into nothing. For four things are observed in vapor:

moisture, coldness, weight [?], and magnitude. Those of these that are opposed to fire are wiped out by the superior force of the prevailing element, for neither moisture nor coldness remains what it was once it comes into fire. Magnitude, however, is akin even to the substance of fire, for fire too is seen to have quantity, and quantity does not fight against quantity. The magnitude of the vapor, then, is preserved, separated from the quality of moist and cold. The quality of weight, which is essentially inherent in the nature of vapor, is preserved together with the magnitude, since heaviness is naturally present equally in moist things and in dry. If this is so, our mind will no longer tire of following the sequence of events, and it can understand how water becomes earth when the vapors change their quality, and so takes on a nature of the same kind as earth. For dry and heavy are the properties of the quality we observe in earth, and it is into this that the vapor was transformed when it was burnt. Having taken hold of this starting point, I think it best not to let go of the sequence of the inquiry, in which our study proceeds through what is probable and leads us by the hand to the truth. This also seems to be why the sea always stays within its own bounds. As waters are continually added to it, a matching amount is drawn off little by little through vapors to the region above, where the warming heat, like a cupping glass, draws up the fine part of the nature of liquids. Someone may object that in the inland and more northern [?] regions the coldness of the surrounding air seems to tell against this argument, because the sea in those parts is not [?] strongly warmed and gives off vapors only sluggishly. This objection can be answered with two arguments. First, the sea is one and continuous with itself throughout. Even though it is divided into countless seas, it is nowhere torn away from its connection with itself. So if the southern sea lies under the continual presence of heat [?], the loss that occurs there is felt in the cold parts, because the water flows over of its own accord, by the downward tendency of its nature, toward the part that is always being moved. Second, the fact that the whole sea is brine, though it comes from all kinds of water, testifies equally to the giving off of vapors, for dryness is the property of the nature of salt. If this quality is mixed equally into the whole sea, then the brine will have the same effect in every part. Every nature always produces the effect that corresponds to its own power. As fire burns, snow chills, and honey sweetens, so salt dries. The drying nature of salt is mixed into the seas everywhere, because divine wisdom provided this to make it easy for vapors to be given off. In a way the brine squeezes and drives all the fine part of the water out of the sea, prevailing over the moisture by the dryness inherent in its nature. It is therefore not unreasonable to think that moisture is consumed equally everywhere, as the air draws up the sea through the

ON THE HEXAEMERON. vapors. Now, all the moisture in the air becomes cloud, and from there rain flows down on the earth. The preceding argument has shown this, and prophecy teaches it as well, attributing such a work to God when it says: "He who calls the water of the sea and pours it out on the face of the earth," and many other things. That all the clouds are baked by the heat above and completely parched we have also learned from what actually happens. It remains, then, not to pass over the objection that naturally arises from what has been said. Someone following what has been examined so far will say: "From the example of the oil we have learned that the material of the substance is not lost even after it has been baked, but passes into the air, turned into earthy matter by the action of fire. But when the moisture has vanished into the opposite quality, how can the moist nature remain undiminished forever? The hot substance is always parching the moisture in the vapors and changing it into a dry quality, as our study has shown step by step through what has been examined. Moisture evaporates, and once it has been divided through the vapors into fine and indivisible pieces, it becomes easy prey for the heat. If so, then since the moist passes into the dry quality, we must consider truer the view that there is a certain abundance of waters that always replenishes what the fire consumes." One might perhaps also find some testimony for this view in Scripture: the floodgates of heaven were opened when the earth was to be submerged, and the water rose far above every mountain peak. But I say that this scriptural objection can be answered by another passage of Scripture, for I know how Scripture customarily uses divine words in a figurative sense. What does it mean by "opening," and what does it indicate by "shutting"? Clearly what is shut is what gets opened, and what is opened is what gets shut. Once, in the time of Elijah, when drought [?] prevailed, Scripture says: "The heaven was shut for three years and six months." I think, then, that when the word of Scripture says the floodgates of heaven were opened, it means opened in the same sense in which heaven was shut during the time of drought. Yet on that occasion, through Elijah's prayer, a cloud rose from the sea and opened heaven for them by bringing rain. This clearly shows that not even then did the firmament of heaven split open and the rain pour down from the waters said to lie above it. Rather, Scripture calls "heaven" the air around the earth, which sets the limit for vapors and is the boundary of the very fine nature that lies above. Beyond it nothing heavier has any power to ascend: no cloud, no wind, no vapor, no exhalation, no bird. So Scripture customarily calls what is overhead "heaven", as when it speaks of the "birds of heaven" that fly through this air. But even if these things are so, our argument has not yet

…has [?] resolved: how is it that changing vapors into something dry does not diminish the moisture, which is used up as the hot substance gains the upper hand? On this point it would be well to find another line of reasoning that fits the inquiry. Perhaps by working at it more diligently we may arrive at [?] an adequate understanding of the question. I have heard the prophecy describe the greatness of God's power through the wonders of creation, where it says: "Who has measured the water with his hand, and the heaven with a span, and all the earth with a handful? Who has set the mountains on a scale, and the valleys on a balance?" By this, I think, the prophet plainly teaches that each of the elements is bounded by its own measures. God's all-embracing power, which he calls hand, handful and span, binds each existing thing within its proper measure. If, then, the heaven has been measured by the divine power, and the water by the hand, and all the earth by the handful; if the valleys are weighed and a clear weight is fixed as the limit of the mountains, then each thing must remain at its own measure and weight. Neither increase nor decrease can occur in things that God has measured and holds in his grasp. The prophecy bears witness that existing things receive neither addition nor reduction. So each thing certainly remains forever at its own measure, while the changeable nature we observe in things turns everything into everything else. It alters each thing into another, and then, by change and alteration, brings it back again from that other to what it was at first. In our earlier discussion, using the example of the oil, we gave a fair account of how this moist vapor passes through the flame and takes on an earthy quality, being turned into something dry as it is baked. Now we should consider the next question. When the matter of the vapor has been altered into the opposite quality, can that remnant of the vapor stay up above? Here the argument has in mind whatever the baking has turned into something finer and less visible. Yet I think we can form a judgment about this too from examples familiar to you. Here too the fine particles of soot do not stay suspended in the air forever. Because the air is thin, they spread [?] toward what is akin to them and stain the ground, the walls and the roof beams. It follows, then, that we should suppose the same about that remnant as well. Isa. [?]

…the encompassing. But he who will be in all things will not be in things that do not exist. — Gregory: "What, then, should we say," I asked, "to those who are faint-hearted about these circumstances?" — Macrina: "Let us say to them," said the teacher, "'It is useless, friends, to chafe and fret at the chain of events that must follow one another. You do not know the goal toward which each particular thing ordered in the universe is moving. By the skilled wisdom of the One who guides all things, everything must be brought into kinship with the divine nature, in a certain order and sequence. This is why rational nature came into being: so that the wealth of divine good things would not lie idle. Rather, the wisdom that established the universe constructed certain vessels endowed with free choice, receptacles [?] for living [?] beings, … [?] ever growing greater by the addition of what is poured in [?]. … [?] For participation in the divine good is such that it makes the one in whom it comes to be greater and more capacious. The receiver takes on increase in power and in size, so that whoever is nourished by it grows and never stops growing. The fountain of good things flows without failing, and nothing the participant receives is superfluous or useless. So its nature turns all that flows in into an increase of its own size, and becomes at once more drawn to what is better and more capacious. Each side advances along with the other. The power that is nourished grows greater through the abundance of good things, and the supply that nourishes overflows in step with the increase of what is growing. It is likely, then, that the soul will rise to such a size that no limit cuts its growth short. With such prospects before us, are you vexed that nature is advancing toward its own goal along the path appointed for us? There is no other way for us to run the course into what lies beyond. This heavy, earthy burden that weighs us down must be shaken off from our soul. By better care we must be cleansed of the attachment to it that we have had in this life. Only then can we, in purity, be joined to what is like us. And if you have some attachment to this body and are grieved at being parted from what you love,'"

For everything will lie entirely with whatever carries it along, and life will be no different from unballasted ships, shifted now to one harbour, now to another, of good or bad fortune, by spontaneous accidents as though by waves. For how is it possible for a man born through vice to be outside it? And how could any deliberate impulse toward the life of virtue arise in a man whose nature, as they say, has its beginning from vice? For just as none of the irrational creatures tries to speak in human fashion, but uses the voice that is native and natural to it and thinks it no loss to lack speech, in the same way those for whom vice is supposed to be the beginning and cause of life would never come to desire virtue, since it would lie outside their nature. Yet for all who have purified their souls by reasoning, the life of virtue is a matter of zeal and desire. By these things, then, it is clearly shown that vice is not older than life, nor did nature take its first beginnings from there; rather, the wisdom of God which orders the universe stands at the beginning of our life. And when the soul has come into being in the way that pleases its Creator, it then chooses with full authority what it wills by its power of choice, and becomes whatever it wishes. We can learn the argument from the example of the eyes: to see belongs to them by nature, not to see comes from choice or from some affliction. For what is contrary to nature can sometimes take the place of nature, either when someone voluntarily shuts his eye, or when he has been deprived of sight through some affliction. …living in darkness, and conversely, when it looks purely toward the truth, it comes to be far from the afflictions of darkness. "When, then," someone will ask, "does it come into being, and how?" But the inquiry into how each thing came to be must be removed from our discussion altogether. For not even with things readily open to our understanding, which we grasp through sense, could searching reason comprehend how the visible thing came to subsist; so much so that not even God-inspired and holy men thought such a thing could be grasped. "By faith we understand," says the Apostle, "that the ages were framed by the word of God, so that what is seen was made from things that do not appear." He would not, I think, have said this if he had believed the object of inquiry could be known by reasoning. But that the age itself, and everything that came to be in it, was framed by the divine will (whatever this age may be, in which the whole of creation, visible and invisible, is contemplated), this the Apostle says he has believed; the how he left unexplored. For I think such a thing cannot be reached by those who search, since the question about these matters presents us with many perplexities: how did the moving come from the stationary nature, the extended and composite from the simple and unextended? From the transcendent essence itself? But that does not agree with beings being of a different kind from it. From somewhere else, then? And yet reason sees nothing outside the divine nature. For our conception would be split into different first principles if anything were thought to lie outside the creative cause, from which its artful wisdom gathers its materials for creation. And the existence of the will is substance. Now since beings are divided in two, into the intelligible and the bodily, the creation of intelligible things does not seem in any way out of harmony with the incorporeal nature; rather, by its nearness it displays what is formless, intangible and unextended — which one would not be wrong to suppose of the transcendent nature too. But bodily creation is seen in properties that have nothing in common with the Divine, and this above all causes great perplexity for reason, which cannot see how the visible comes from the invisible, the solid and resistant from the intangible, the bounded from the unbounded, and from what is without quantity and magnitude that which is wholly encompassed by measures observed in quantity — and likewise with each of the things perceived in bodily nature. About these we say this much: that none of the things observed in a body is by itself body — not shape, not colour, not weight, not extension, not size, nor anything else observed as a quality — but each of them is a concept; and their concurrence and union with one another becomes body.
